newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi gold demand seen poised for strong growth.
newsitem.headline: Saudi gold demand seen poised for strong growth.

text.p: Saudi Arabian gold demand could show double-digit growth over each of the next five years, reaching 350 to 400 tonnes by 2002-2003 from a current 237 tonnes, a United Nations consultant said on Sunday.

"In my view, if the oil price is sustained, (Saudi gold) demand should grow 10 percent for the next five years," Shyam Mandawat, a U.N. gold market observer, said on the sidelines of a gold conference in the Gulf Arab emirate of Dubai.
Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer and exporter, is the biggest Middle East consumer of the yellow metal and is enjoying an economic upturn thanks to higher oil prices in recent years.
A rise in the oil price to around $18-20 a barrel from $14 had boosted disposable income in the oil state, Mandawat said.

Tony Warwick-Ching of British consultants CRU International said Saudi gold demand for jewellery manufacture had already experienced annual growth of up to 16 percent since 1980, versus industry-wide growth of 3.2 percent.
There are some 40 gold factories in the kingdom, the vast majority of which came into business only in the mid-1980s.

Mandawat saw demand growth in the kingdom, where its population of 18 million is growing at around 3.5 to four percent a year, would be led by customer preferences for novel and frequently changing jewellery designs.
Jewellery accounts for roughly 80 percent of total gold use.

"A Saudi housewife is the largest buyer of jewellery and she wants the latest fashions which change every three months," Mandawat said. "The potential of Saudi Arabia as a gold jewellery consumer is terrific. Consumption is going to multiply at a very high rate."

Even though the wearing of gold jewellery by men is not compatible with strict Islamic sharia law, gold demand is fanned by the same law that allows a man to have up to four wives at any one time on condition they are equally treated.

Meantime the World Gold Council, a producer group which seeks to promote the metal, has in recent years effectively widened its sales appeal to children -- which make up half the kingdom's population -- by introducing a range of jewellery featuring colourful cartoon characters.

Jewellery consumption in the kingdom led by demand for 21 carat bangles, weighing on average 15 grammes, and five-piece individual jewellery sets reached 180-200 tonnes last year, according to Mandawat.
Most of this demand -- 160 tonnes -- was imported from Italy, Singapore, India and Turkey while local Saudi factories supplied a further 40 tonnes to the local market, he said.

Consumption in Saudi Arabia ran at about eight grammes per head, according to figures presented to the conference by Warwick-Ching. This compared with a ratio in India of a one gramme purchase per five people, according to Mandawat.
Gold mines in Saudi Arabia produce eight tonnes a year, all of which is sold to the Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency (SAMA), the kingdom's central bank.
